section_title: How can teachers stand in the way of the truth they teach?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 45 One of the experts in the law told Him, “Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well.” 46 “Woe to you as well, experts in the law!” He replied. “For you weigh men down with heavy burdens, but you yourselves will not lift a finger to lighten their load. 47 Woe to you! For you build tombs for the prophets, but it was your fathers who killed them. 48 So you are witnesses consenting to the deeds of your fathers: They killed the prophets, and you build their tombs.

49 Because of this, the wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles; some of them they will kill and others they will persecute.’ 50 As a result, this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets that has been shed since the foundation of the world, 51 from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, all of it will be charged to this generation. 52 Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key to knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering.”
53 As Jesus went on from there, the scribes and Pharisees began to oppose Him bitterly and to ply Him with questions about many things, 54 waiting to catch Him in something He might say.

context_lines: An expert in the law objects that Jesus’ words insult his group too. Jesus responds with three further warnings directed to these experts.

First, they place heavy burdens on people without helping to carry them. Second, they build tombs for prophets whom their ancestors killed. Jesus exposes a continuing pattern: people may honor the memory of God’s messengers while resisting those He sends in their own time.

He speaks of prophets and apostles being sent, killed and persecuted, and of this generation’s accountability for the blood of the prophets, from Abel to Zechariah. The warning joins the present response to a long history of resistance to God’s word.

The final charge concerns the key to knowledge. The experts have failed to enter and have hindered others who were entering. The chapter closes with scribes and Pharisees questioning Jesus bitterly and trying to catch Him in something He says. Their response continues the resistance He has just described.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly see a warning about teachers who burden others, resist God’s messengers and obstruct understanding. Wesley connects the key to knowledge with knowing the Messiah, while the Catholic bishops’ notes connect the sending of prophets and apostles with the continuing mission and its opposition. ([Wesley on Luke 11:46–52](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-luke/); [USCCB notes on Luke 11:45–52](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/luke/11))
god_plan_lines: Jesus explicitly joins the sending of prophets and apostles in this warning. Hebrews describes God speaking through the prophets and then through His Son. The present encounter therefore belongs within the larger question of how people receive God’s message as it reaches them through Christ. ([Luke 11:49–52](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/11.htm); [Hebrews 1:1–3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/1.htm))

Acts gives a later example in Stephen’s testimony. He recalls the persecution of the prophets and confronts his hearers’ resistance to the Holy Spirit; they then kill him. Even while being stoned, he prays to Jesus and asks that the sin not be held against them. The witness continues amid the very opposition Jesus describes. ([Acts 7:51–60](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/7.htm))
